claim: HCN ion channels open on hyperpolarization, in contrast to most voltage-gated ion channels.
source: In contrast to most voltage-gated ion channels, hyperpolarization- and cAMP gated (HCN) ion channels open on hyperpolarization.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and is established knowledge in the field.

claim: All-atom molecular dynamics simulations of HCN1 channel under hyperpolarization reveal an initial downward movement of the S4 voltage-sensor.
source: All-atom molecular dynamics simulations (~20 μs) of HCN1 channel under hyperpolarization reveals an initial downward movement of the S4 voltage-sensor but following the transfer of last gating charge, the S4 breaks into two sub-helices with the lower sub-helix becoming parallel to the membrane.
evidence: This claim is supported by the molecular dynamics simulation data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Following the transfer of the last gating charge, the S4 breaks into two sub-helices with the lower sub-helix becoming parallel to the membrane.
source: All-atom molecular dynamics simulations (~20 μs) of HCN1 channel under hyperpolarization reveals an initial downward movement of the S4 voltage-sensor but following the transfer of last gating charge, the S4 breaks into two sub-helices with the lower sub-helix becoming parallel to the membrane.
evidence: This is a key finding from the molecular dynamics simulations shown in Figure 1.

claim: The gating polarity strongly correlates with helical turn propensity of the substituents at the breakpoint.
source: Functional studies on bipolar channels show that the gating polarity strongly correlates with helical turn propensity of the substituents at the breakpoint.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5 demonstrating correlation between gating polarity index and turn propensity.

claim: In a proto-HCN background, the replacement of breakpoint serine with a bulky hydrophobic amino acid is sufficient to completely flip the gating polarity from inward to outward-rectifying.
source: Remarkably, in a proto-HCN background, the replacement of breakpoint serine with a bulky hydrophobic amino acid is sufficient to completely flip the gating polarity from inward to outward-rectifying.
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 5C with the EEHEH chimera.

claim: HCN channels are found in the pacemaking cells of heart and brain where they play a singular role in regulating rhythmic electrical oscillations.
source: The hyperpolarization-activated and cyclic nucleotide activated ion channels are found in the pacemaking cells of heart and brain where they play a singular role in regulating rhythmic electrical oscillations (Brown et al., 1979; Ludwig et al., 1998; Santoro et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: HCN channels open at membrane potentials below the threshold of action potential and depolarize the membrane by increasing the permeability to Na+ ions.
source: Unlike other members of the voltage-gated ion channel family, these channels open at membrane potentials below the threshold of action potential and depolarize the membrane by increasing the permeability to Na+ ions (Brown et al., 1979).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Brown et al., 1979.

claim: The slow gating kinetics and low permeability of HCN channels determine the frequency of action potential spikes.
source: Their slow gating kinetics and low permeability determine the frequency of action potential spikes (Larson et al., 2013; Sharpe et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The gating properties of HCN channels are regulated by PIP2 and second messengers such as cAMP.
source: In addition to voltage, the gating properties of these channels are regulated by PIP2 and second messengers such as cAMP which mediates the 'fight or flight' response by increasing the activity of HCN channels in sinoatrial nodal cells of the heart (Brown et al., 1979; Pian et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: HCN channels are tetrameric and each subunit consists of a voltage-sensing domain (VSD) (S1-S4 helices) and pore-forming domain (S5-S6 helices).
source: They are tetrameric and each subunit consists of a voltage-sensing domain (VSD) (S1-S4 helices) and pore-forming domain (S5-S6 helices) (Lee and MacKinnon, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the HCN1 structure paper.

claim: The VSD and pore domain (PD) of HCN channels are arranged in a non-domain swapped arrangement.
source: Like other members of CNBD family, the VSD and pore domain (PD) are arranged in a non-domain swapped arrangement (Lee and MacKinnon, 2017; Whicher and MacKinnon, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to structural studies.

claim: The S4 segment of HCN1 channel is at least two helical turns longer than the corresponding S4 in depolarization activated ion channels.
source: First, the S4 segment of HCN1 channel is at least two helical turns longer than the corresponding S4 in depolarization activated ion channels.
evidence: This is based on structural comparison with other voltage-gated channels.

claim: At the cytosolic amino terminal end, a 45 residue stretch forms a small 3-helix bundle which interacts with the voltage-sensor and CNBD domain, called the HCN domain.
source: Second, at the cytosolic amino terminal end, a 45 residue stretch forms a small 3-helix bundle which interacts with the voltage-sensor and CNBD domain. This domain is unique to this channel family and is called the HCN domain.
evidence: This is based on the HCN1 structure.

claim: The S4 helix of the HCN1 channel is in tight juxtaposition with the S5 helix, unlike in the related depolarization activated ether-á-go-go (EAG) channel.
source: Finally, the S4 helix of the HCN1 channel is in tight juxtaposition with the S5 helix, unlike in the related depolarization activated ether-á-go-go (EAG) channel (Lee and MacKinnon, 2017).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison between HCN1 and EAG channels.

claim: The voltage-sensing domains of the HCN channels have an intrinsic ability to drive the channel in both hyperpolarizing and depolarizing directions.
source: Recent studies show that the voltage-sensing domains of the HCN channels have an intrinsic ability to drive the channel in both hyperpolarizing and depolarizing directions (Cowgill et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study by the authors.

claim: The ability to open the channel on hyperpolarization neither depends on the extra length of the S4 segment nor on the HCN domain.
source: This ability to open the channel on hyperpolarization neither depends on the extra length of the S4 segment nor on the HCN domain suggesting that there are other non-obvious determinants of gating polarity in the voltage-sensing S4 of HCN channels.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Cowgill et al., 2019.

claim: Cysteine accessibility studies show that the S4 undergoes a large downward motion much like the voltage-sensor of the Shaker potassium channel.
source: Cysteine accessibility studies to probe the nature of these conformational changes show that the S4 undergoes a large downward motion much like the voltage-sensor of the Shaker potassium channel (Bell et al., 2004; Männikkö et al., 2002; Vemana et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous cysteine accessibility studies.

claim: The residues in the top part of the S4 helix showed larger displacements compared to those at the lower end.
source: One notable difference, however, is that the residues in the top part of the S4 helix showed larger displacements compared to those at the lower end.
evidence: This is based on previous cysteine accessibility studies.

claim: Transition metal FRET studies propose that the S4 undergoes a downward motion with a slight bend at the tail end of the S4 helix.
source: Recently, transition metal FRET studies also propose that the S4 undergoes a downward motion with a slight bend at the tail end of the S4 helix (Dai et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Dai et al., 2019.

claim: Two independent runs of tens of microseconds long molecular dynamics (MD) simulations were carried out using the special purpose Anton 2 supercomputer.
source: In order to probe the structural transitions through the gating cycle, we took advantage of the special purpose Anton 2 supercomputer (Shaw et al., 2014) to carry out two independent runs of tens of microseconds long molecular dynamics (MD) simulations.
evidence: This describes the computational methods used in the study.

claim: The simulations showed that the downward movement of the voltage-sensors is accompanied by breaking of the S4 helix into two sub-helices.
source: Our simulations showed that the downward movement of the voltage-sensors is accompanied by breaking of the S4 helix into two sub-helices and the lower sub-helix adopting an orientation parallel to the membrane plane and turning into a surrogate S4-S5 linker.
evidence: This is a key finding from the MD simulations.

claim: The lower sub-helix adopts an orientation parallel to the membrane plane and turns into a surrogate S4-S5 linker.
source: Our simulations showed that the downward movement of the voltage-sensors is accompanied by breaking of the S4 helix into two sub-helices and the lower sub-helix adopting an orientation parallel to the membrane plane and turning into a surrogate S4-S5 linker.
evidence: This is a key finding from the MD simulations.

claim: Bipolar chimeras were utilized which exhibit both hyperpolarization and depolarization-activated currents.
source: To probe the importance of this helix breaking transition, we utilized bipolar chimeras which exhibit both hyperpolarization and depolarization-activated currents (Cowgill et al., 2019).
evidence: This describes the experimental approach used to test the helix breaking model.

claim: Both the location of the breakpoint and nature of amino acid therein is critical for gating polarity in the channels of this superfamily.
source: Our studies reveal that both the location of the breakpoint and nature of amino acid therein is critical for gating polarity in the channels of this superfamily.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Strongly hyperpolarizing conditions (−550 mV) were applied to accelerate channel kinetics in simulations.
source: First, we applied strongly hyperpolarizing conditions (−550 mV) similar to the approach used for simulations of Kv1.2/2.1 deactivation (Jensen et al., 2012).
evidence: This describes a methodological approach used in the simulations.

claim: A mutant (M153T/I160V) was designed to increase hydrophilicity in the VSD and facilitate the movement of gating charges.
source: Inspired by the work of Lacroix et al. (2013), we designed a mutant that was anticipated to increase hydrophilicity in the VSD.
evidence: This describes the rationale for the mutations introduced in the simulations.

claim: The mutant (M153T/I160V) showed signs of faster activation than the wild type (WT) channel in preliminary simulations.
source: In agreement with our prediction, the mutant showed signs of faster activation than the wild type (WT) channel (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), therefore we proceeded to run Anton simulations with the mutant channel.
evidence: This is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The M153T/I160V mutations are well tolerated functionally.
source: Functional testing shows that these mutations are well tolerated (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Substantial conformational change was observed in 6 out of 8 voltage sensors from two independent ~20 µs simulations of the full length channel.
source: Substantial conformational change was observed in 6 out of 8 voltage sensors from two independent ~20 µs simulations of the full length channel (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the MD simulations shown in Figure 1.

claim: A large downward movement of the S4 helix drives two positively charged residues across the focused electric field at the charge transfer center (F186).
source: A large downward movement of the S4 helix drives two positively charged residues across the focused electric field at the charge transfer center (F186) (Figure 1A,C).
evidence: This is shown in the simulation data in Figure 1A,C.

claim: The large vertical movement of S4 agrees with previous predictions based on cysteine accessibility and voltage clamp fluorometry.
source: This large vertical movement agrees with previous predictions based on cysteine accessibility (Bell et al., 2004; Vemana et al., 2004) and voltage clamp fluorometry (Dai et al., 2019).
evidence: This compares the simulation results with previous experimental studies.

claim: The simulations reveal an unexpected break in the S4 helix when the last gating charge is transferred.
source: However, the simulations reveal an unexpected break in the S4 helix, causing the C-terminal half to adopt an orientation parallel to the membrane plane (Figure 1A–E, Video 1) when the last gating charge is transferred.
evidence: This is a key finding from the MD simulations shown in Figure 1 and Video 1.

claim: Overlay of 6 independent voltage sensors confirms that they converge to the same activated (Down) structure.
source: Overlay of 6 independent voltage sensors confirms that they converge to the same activated (Down) structure (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The helix breaking model is in stark contrast to what has previously been observed in simulations of voltage-gated potassium channels and new resting state structures of voltage-gated sodium channels.
source: This helix breaking model is in stark contrast to what has previously been observed in simulations of voltage-gated potassium channels and new resting state structures of voltage-gated sodium channels (Delemotte et al., 2011; Amaral et al., 2012; Jensen et al., 2012; Vargas et al., 2012; She et al., 2018; Xu et al., 2019; Wisedchaisri et al., 2019).
evidence: This compares the current findings with previous studies on other voltage-gated channels.

claim: In voltage-gated potassium and sodium channels, the consensus view is that S4 moves vertically and twists as a unit in what is typically referred to as the helical screw model.
source: In these channels, the consensus view is that S4 moves vertically and twists as a unit in what is typically referred to as the helical screw model (Figure 1E).
evidence: This describes the established model for other voltage-gated channels.

claim: The structure of the cyclic nucleotide-gated (CNG) channel TAX4 shows a bent S4 helix reminiscent of what is observed for HCN1.
source: Interestingly, the structure of the cyclic nucleotide-gated (CNG) channel TAX4 (Li et al., 2017), a close relative to HCN channels (Baker et al., 2015), shows a bent S4 helix reminiscent of what we observe for HCN1 (Figure 1D,E).
evidence: This is based on comparison with the TAX4 structure shown in Figure 1D,E.

claim: The S4 segment in HCN and TAX4 channels may have an intrinsic propensity to bend.
source: Thus, the S4 segment in these two closely related clades may have an intrinsic propensity to bend.
evidence: This is inferred from the similarity between HCN1 simulations and TAX4 structure.

claim: The net gating charge per VSD is 1.85 eo (or 7.4 eo per channel).
source: Summing the contribution of each residue shows the net gating charge per VSD is 1.85 eo (or 7.4 eo per channel), which is in good agreement with the eight charges per channel suggested previously through kinetic modeling of HCN channels activation (Hummert et al., 2018).
evidence: This is calculated from the simulations and compared with previous kinetic modeling.

claim: The per-residue contribution to gating charge is dominated by the two positively charged residues on S4 (R267 and K270) which move relative to the charge transfer center.
source: As expected, the per-residue contribution to this charge difference is dominated by the two positively charged residues on S4 (R267 and K270) which move relative to the charge transfer center, with lower contributions from the other charges of S4 (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is shown in the gating charge analysis in Figure 1F.

claim: The negative countercharges on S1-S3 contribute to the net gating charge.
source: Additionally, the negative countercharges on S1-S3 contribute to the net gating charge as was experimentally shown for the Shaker potassium channel (Seoh et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by comparison with previous experimental work on Shaker.

claim: The acidic residues of S1-S3 contribute to the gating charge despite little to no net displacement.
source: Interestingly, the acidic residues of S1-S3 contribute to the gating charge despite little to no net displacement (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The contribution of acidic residues to gating charge implies a redistribution of the local electric field inside the VSD upon activation.
source: This implies a redistribution of the local electric field inside the VSD upon activation, as previously suggested based on HCN1 cysteine accessibility studies (Bell et al., 2004).
evidence: This is inferred from the gating charge analysis and supported by previous studies.

claim: The hydration profile of the VSD is altered upon activation.
source: The local electric field within the VSD is thought to be controlled primarily by hydration of the water accessible crevices (Islas and Sigworth, 2001); as expected, the hydration profile of the VSD is altered upon activation (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1H and supported by previous theoretical work.

claim: The increase in hydration of the activated state may come from the mutations introduced to accelerate gating kinetics.
source: It is possible that the increase in hydration of the activated state comes from the mutations we introduced to accelerate gating kinetics.
evidence: This is speculation about the origin of increased hydration.

claim: Inward movement of the S4 positive charges may cause an increase in hydration of the countercharges on S1-S3.
source: Alternatively, inward movement of the S4 positive charges may cause an increase in hydration of the countercharges on S1-S3 (Seoh et al., 1996).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The increased hydration on the internal side is likely related to the broadening of the internal crevice due to S4 bending.
source: On the internal side, the increased hydration is likely related to the broadening of the internal crevice due to S4 bending.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural changes observed in the simulations.

claim: The experimentally-attained accessibility of most S4 residues agrees well with the accessibility pattern predicted from the simulation model.
source: The experimentally-attained accessibility of most of these residues agrees well with the accessibility pattern predicted from our model (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is shown by comparison of experimental and computational data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: There is a much larger change in accessibility for the internally accessible residues than external, indicating a larger conformational change in the internal crevice.
source: A key feature of this pattern is that there is a much larger change in accessibility for the internally accessible residues than external. This indicates that there is a larger conformational change in the internal crevice and lends support to the S4 bending movement observed in our simulations.
evidence: This is inferred from the accessibility data.

claim: The simulation predicts an increase in the accessibility of S1-S3 upon activation due to broadening of the internally facing crevice.
source: In addition to the state-dependent accessibilities in S4, the simulation also predicts an increase in the accessibility of S1-S3 upon activation. These arise due to broadening of the internally facing crevice and would not be expected if S4 moved vertically as a unit (Figure 2A,B, see also Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This is a prediction from the simulations shown in Figure 2.

claim: In the activated state models, even the charge-transfer center (F186) becomes accessible in 3 out of the six activated states.
source: Surprisingly, in the activated state models extracted from the simulations, even the charge-transfer center (F186) becomes accessible in 3 out of the six activated states (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2C from the simulation analysis.

claim: The WT spHCN channel shows no detectable functional change following MTSET application to either the closed or open states.
source: The WT spHCN channel shows no detectable functional change following MTSET application to either the closed (depolarized) or open (hyperpolarized) states as has been shown previously (Figure 2D and Männikkö et al., 2002).
evidence: This is shown experimentally in Figure 2D and supported by previous work.

claim: In the F186C mutant, internal application of MTSET at depolarized potentials leads to very slowly evolving increase in current amplitude (τmodification=7.5±0.5 M−1s−1).
source: In the charge-transfer center mutant (F186C), internal application of MTSET at depolarized potentials leads to very slowly evolving increase in current amplitude (τmodification=7.5±0.5 M−1s−1).
evidence: This is experimental data from cysteine accessibility measurements.

claim: The charge-transfer center has low solvent accessibility in the resting state.
source: This confirms that the charge-transfer center has low solvent accessibility in the resting state.
evidence: This is inferred from the slow modification rate in the F186C mutant.

claim: Application of MTSET to F186C during hyperpolarization results in a rapid increase in peak current amplitude (τmodification=440±30 M−1s−1).
source: In contrast, application of MTSET during hyperpolarization results in a rapid increase in peak current amplitude that quickly reaches a steady state (τmodification=440±30 M−1s−1).
evidence: This is experimental data from cysteine accessibility measurements.

claim: The more than an order of magnitude increase in accessibility of the charge-transfer center upon channel activation is difficult to reconcile with the helical screw model and supports the helix-breaking model.
source: This more than an order of magnitude increase in accessibility of the charge-transfer center upon channel activation is difficult to reconcile with the helical screw model and supports the helix-breaking model predicted by the simulations.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: The HEHEH chimera containing the S3b-S4 voltage-sensing segment from HCN1 activates only upon hyperpolarization.
source: The HEHEH chimera containing the S3b-S4 voltage-sensing segment from HCN1 activates only upon hyperpolarization while the HEEEH containing the S3b-S4 voltage-sensing segment from the depolarization-activated EAG channel activates only on depolarization.
evidence: This is experimental data from the chimera studies.

claim: The HEEEH chimera containing the S3b-S4 voltage-sensing segment from EAG activates only on depolarization.
source: The HEHEH chimera containing the S3b-S4 voltage-sensing segment from HCN1 activates only upon hyperpolarization while the HEEEH containing the S3b-S4 voltage-sensing segment from the depolarization-activated EAG channel activates only on depolarization.
evidence: This is experimental data from the chimera studies.

claim: The chimera with only the lower paddle of HCN1 activates primarily upon hyperpolarization.
source: Indeed, the chimera with only the lower paddle of HCN1 activates primarily upon hyperpolarization.
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The upper paddle chimera activates only upon depolarization and its behavior closely resembles that of the parent chimera with the full EAG voltage sensor.
source: On the other hand, the upper paddle chimera activates only upon depolarization and its behavior closely resembles that of the parent chimera with the full EAG voltage sensor.
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The source of inverted gating polarity can be localized to the lower portion of S4, precisely where the helix break is observed in simulations.
source: Together, these results suggest that the source of inverted gating polarity can be localized to the lower portion of S4, precisely where we observe the helix break in our simulations.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the chimera experiments.

claim: The S4 helix breaks in a highly consistent location centered at L271.
source: A closer examination of the models from the simulations reveals that the S4 helix breaks in a highly consistent location centered at L271 (Figure 3B,C).
evidence: This is shown in the simulation analysis in Figure 3B,C.

claim: Position L271 is predominantly conserved between HCN and EAG families.
source: Comparison of the consensus sequences for HCN and EAG channels show that this position is predominantly conserved between families.
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment analysis.

claim: The overall sequence in the S4 breakpoint region is very similar between HCN and EAG with the exception of position 272.
source: In fact, the overall sequence in this region is very similar between HCN and EAG with the exception of position 272.
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The consensus for HCN channels at position 272 is polar (such as serine for HCN1) whereas the consensus for EAG is hydrophobic.
source: The consensus for HCN channels at this position is polar (such as serine for HCN1) whereas the consensus for EAG is hydrophobic.
evidence: This is based on sequence alignment analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Position 272 is situated directly adjacent to the helix break, suggesting it may serve a vital role in channel gating.
source: Furthermore, this residue is situated directly adjacent to the helix break, suggesting it may serve a vital role in channel gating.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural analysis.

claim: The lack of functional expression of mutants with hydrophobic residues at position 272 in WT HCN1 indicates that serine is critical for HCN1 channel gating.
source: The lack of functional expression of mutants with hydrophobic residues at position 272 indicates that serine is critical for HCN1 channel gating but we must rule out the possibility that these channels are simply not trafficked to the membrane.
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: For the hydrophobic mutations at S272, surface fluorescence is observed well above the background of uninjected oocytes, yet no currents are observed.
source: For the hydrophobic mutations, we observe surface fluorescence well above the background of uninjected oocytes, yet we still do not observe currents in these oocytes (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–C.

claim: The lack of currents detected in S272 hydrophobic mutants is due to non-functional channels and does not reflect a trafficking defect.
source: This confirms that the lack of currents detected in these mutants is due to non-functional channels and does not reflect a trafficking defect.
evidence: This is concluded from the surface expression data.

claim: The S272L mutant in the HHHEH bipolar background is a predominantly outwardly rectifying channel in contrast to the parent HHHEH.
source: Strikingly, the S272L mutant is a predominantly outwardly rectifying channel in contrast to the parent HHHEH.
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Only the L271S mutation was capable of restoring a primarily hyperpolarization-activated phenotype like the HHHEH parent.
source: Interestingly, only the L271S mutation was capable of restoring a primarily hyperpolarization-activated phenotype like the HHHEH parent (Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E)).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The location of the serine in the S4 helix is critical for the inverted channel gating phenotype.
source: This suggests that the location of the serine in the S4 helix is critical for the inverted channel gating phenotype.
evidence: This is concluded from the mutagenesis data.

claim: The free energy difference between the activation of HCN1 and its S272L mutant is 0.7 ± 0.4 kcal/mol per VSD.
source: The estimated free energy difference of 0.7 ± 0.4 kcal/mol equates to ~2.8 kcal/mol per channel suggesting that the S272L mutation shifts the equilibrium toward the resting state, thus disfavoring the bending motion.
evidence: This is calculated from free energy perturbation simulations.

claim: The S272L mutation shifts the equilibrium toward the resting state, thus disfavoring the bending motion.
source: The estimated free energy difference of 0.7 ± 0.4 kcal/mol equates to ~2.8 kcal/mol per channel suggesting that the S272L mutation shifts the equilibrium toward the resting state, thus disfavoring the bending motion.
evidence: This is inferred from the free energy calculations.

claim: The observed difference in free energy is significant because the experimentally determined coupling energy between voltage sensor and pore for spHCN is only 1.3 kT (~0.8 kcal/mol).
source: The observed difference in free energy is significant because the experimentally determined coupling energy between voltage sensor and pore for spHCN is only 1.3 kT (~0.8 kcal/mol) (Ryu and Yellen, 2012)
evidence: This compares the calculated free energy with previous experimental measurements.

claim: Both HHHEH and HHHEΔC SD bipolar constructs showed a clear trend where hydrophobic substitutions favor depolarization activation while hydrophilic substitutions favor hyperpolarization activation.
source: Both constructs tested showed a clear trend where hydrophobic substitutions favor depolarization activation while hydrophilic substitutions favor hyperpolarization activation.
evidence: This is shown in the experimental data in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The gating polarity index (PO-150 mV/ PO50 mV) is inversely correlated with residue hydrophobicity with a tight fit.
source: This parameter, which we refer to as the gating polarity index, is inversely correlated with residue hydrophobicity with a tight fit (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is shown in the correlation analysis in Figure 5B.

claim: The negative trend between gating polarity index and hydrophobicity may be caused by the helix-stabilizing nature of hydrophobic residues in transmembrane segments.
source: Previous work on model helices showed that the helical propensity is directly correlated to hydrophobicity in membrane environments (Li and Deber, 1994). Therefore, the negative trend we observed between gating polarity index and hydrophobicity may be caused by the helix-stabilizing nature of hydrophobic residues in transmembrane segments.
evidence: This is inferred from previous work on helical propensity.

claim: The strong, negative correlation is upheld when comparing the gating polarity index to an experimentally-derived scale for transmembrane helical propensity.
source: Indeed, the strong, negative correlation is upheld when comparing the gating polarity index to an experimentally-derived scale for transmembrane helical propensity (Liu and Deber, 1998).
evidence: This is shown in the correlation analysis in Figure 5B.

claim: The gating polarity index shows positive correlation to the independently-derived turn propensity.
source: Finally, the gating polarity index shows positive correlation to the independently-derived turn propensity (Monné et al., 1999), which has previously been used as a metric for helix breaking proclivity.
evidence: This is shown in the correlation analysis in Figure 5B.

claim: These correlations offer strong support for the helix breaking model and reveal that residue polarity at S272 is central to the gating mechanism of HCN channels.
source: Together, these correlations offer strong support for our helix breaking model and reveal that residue polarity at S272 is central to the gating mechanism of HCN channels.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the correlation analyses.

claim: The G362S mutant of hEAG1 shows depolarization-dependent opening with no signs of hyperpolarization activation.
source: The G362S mutant of hEAG1 shows depolarization-dependent opening with no signs of hyperpolarization activation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The leucine, valine, and isoleucine mutations at S272 in the EEHEH background eliminate all detectable hyperpolarization activation, transforming an HCN-like parent into an EAG-like channel with a single point mutation.
source: Remarkably, the leucine, valine, and isoleucine mutations in this background eliminate all detectable hyperpolarization activation in the EEHEH background, transforming an HCN-like parent into an EAG-like channel with a single point mutation (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Divergence of hyperpolarization-activated channels from depolarization-activated channels could have occurred through a single point mutation in the S4 segment.
source: Thus, divergence of hyperpolarization-activated channels from depolarization-activated channels could have occurred through a single point mutation in the S4 segment.
evidence: This is speculation based on the experimental results.

claim: The down state model of the S4 voltage-sensor is consistent with existing S4 cysteine accessibility and transition metal FRET data.
source: Our down state model of the S4 voltage-sensor is consistent with existing S4 cysteine accessibility (Bell et al., 2004; Vemana et al., 2004) and transition metal FRET data (Dai et al., 2019).
evidence: This compares the simulation model with previous experimental data.

claim: The predicted state-dependent accessibility of the residues in the gating scaffold is incompatible with the classical helical screw motion observed in voltage-gated potassium and sodium channels.
source: However, the predicted state-dependent accessibility of the residues in the gating scaffold is incompatible with the classical helical screw motion observed in voltage-gated potassium and sodium channels (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C), see also Pathak et al. (2007).
evidence: This is based on comparison of accessibility predictions with the helical screw model.

claim: The charge transfer center of HCN channels exhibits a distinct pattern of accessibility consistent with the molecular simulations.
source: Our studies show that the charge transfer center of HCN channels exhibit a distinct pattern of accessibility consistent with the molecular simulations.
evidence: This is based on the experimental cysteine accessibility data.

claim: The helix breaking transition is necessary for inward rectification.
source: Furthermore, we find that this helix breaking transition is necessary for inward rectification and our studies show that the gating polarity strongly correlates with the energetics of transmembrane helix formation.
evidence: This is concluded from the mutagenesis and correlation studies.

claim: In a proto-HCN background, the nature of the residue in the S4 breakpoint is the central determinant of gating polarity.
source: Strikingly, in a proto-HCN background, the nature of the residue in the S4 breakpoint is the central determinant of gating polarity and the direction of rectification can be switched by a single amino acid substitution.
evidence: This is concluded from the EEHEH chimera experiments.

claim: The emerging consensus in the field is that VSD activation involves a helical screw motion across the membrane relative to the surrounding S1-S3 bundle.
